channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Manufacturing
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Boston Scientific cannot process or ship orders after a cyberattack — and containment, not the plant floor, is why
item.description: Boston Scientific detected a cyberattack on 25 August and disclosed it the next day; five days on, order processing and shipping are still disrupted and the company has not committed to a restoration date. Manufacturing staff at its Cork, Ireland sites have been sent home because they cannot work, and hospitals are reporting delays to pacemaker and cardiac stent deliveries. Analysts at Piper Sandler said, after speaking with management on 27 August, that the company may resume shipping across all product lines in under three weeks. Ransomware involvement, initial access and data theft remain unconfirmed. For manufacturers the lesson repeats the one Data I/O supplied earlier this month: an intrusion that never touches a control system still stops product leaving the building, because order management, warehouse execution and shipping ride on the enterprise stack that containment isolates first. - Boston Scientific 8-K filing and company statement — reported by Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch and MedTech Dive; Cork plant impact and the analyst estimate via CBS News and Piper Sandler commentary of 27 Aug - Attack detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; still disrupting order processing and shipping as of 28 Aug 2026; no restoration date announced

item.title: [Critical] A chip-programming supplier pulled its own production and shipping systems offline to contain ransomware
item.category: Incident — Ransomware, production and shipping systems taken offline
item.description: Data I/O, which builds the programming systems used to load firmware onto automotive and consumer electronics before assembly, detected ransomware on IT systems on 16 August and disclosed it in an 8-K filed with the SEC on 21 August. Containment involved taking systems offline, and the company said the outage affected shipping, manufacturing, production and support functions. More than 65% of its second-quarter business came from automotive electronics production. The point for a plant manager is second-order: this is a supplier whose downtime shows up as missing programmed parts on someone else’s line, and the disruption came from the containment decision as much as from the malware. The company has since said the incident was contained and systems restored. - Data I/O SEC 8-K filed 21 Aug 2026 — reported by The Record, SecurityWeek and CyberScoop - Ransomware detected 16 Aug 2026; SEC filing 21 Aug 2026; company subsequently reported containment and restoration

item.title: [Critical] FBI seizes the Chinese scanning and relay platforms built out of other people’s IoT devices
item.category: Incident — Law-enforcement action against state-sponsored infrastructure
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms operated by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan handled reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so traffic appeared to come from ordinary domestic addresses. Both are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware. Named victims are federal, but the relay design is the manufacturing lesson: unmanaged internet-connected devices in a plant — cameras, badge readers, HVAC controllers, machine-monitoring gateways — are exactly what these platforms recruited, and your firewall logs never showed who was really there. - US Department of Justice press release and unsealed court documents — corroborated by TechCrunch and UPI - Seizures announced and confirmed 26 Aug 2026; described activity dates from at least 2018 to 2026

item.title: [Critical] Clop has named more than 40 PTC Windchill victims, and what it took is how your products are built
item.category: Incident — PLM supply-chain campaign with named victims
item.description: The Clop extortion group has listed over 40 organisations as victims of a campaign against internet-facing PTC Windchill product lifecycle management deployments, with manufacturing, aerospace and industrial suppliers among the confirmed names. Windchill is where design files, bills of material, supplier documentation, tolerances and change history live. Losing it is not a privacy incident. It is the disclosure of how a product is made, to whom it is sourced, and where the process is sensitive — and for firms whose competitive position rests on process knowledge rather than a patent, that is the whole asset. The campaign also demonstrates the pattern: attackers now go after the engineering record rather than the shop floor. - Clop leak-site listings analysed by security researchers, with PTC vendor guidance — via Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek - Victim listings expanded 15 Aug 2026; PTC guidance issued earlier in August; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] An attacker crossed a shared private cellular network from one operator’s site into another’s plant
item.category: Incident — Lateral movement across a shared carrier network
item.description: CERT Polska’s follow-up report describes an intrusion that started at a wind farm and ended at an unrelated combined heat and power plant, where a turbine was taken out of service. The bridge was a private APN both organisations bought from the same carrier. A private APN is an addressing and billing arrangement, not a security boundary: if the devices on it can reach one another, another subscriber’s compromised router becomes your ingress. Manufacturers should read this as a warning about a common convenience — the cellular links used for remote machine monitoring, OEM diagnostics, outbuildings, tank farms and satellite sites are frequently on exactly this kind of shared arrangement. - CERT Polska incident follow-up report — via Help Net Security, BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Incident 29 Dec 2025; CERT Polska disclosure 8 Aug 2026; press analysis 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
item.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting
item.description: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. No victims, actors or techniques are named. For a plant the useful part is the instruction not to assume OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure arises through misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. In discrete and process manufacturing that usually means a specific short list: the machine an OEM ships with its own 4G router for remote support, the line acquired with a business unit and never brought under the standard build, the engineering workstation dual-homed for convenience, and the cell that still speaks Modbus or unauthenticated S7comm because the migration project was deferred. It lands the same week five US agencies described AI-written scripts reading S7 controllers across critical manufacturing. - UK National Cyber Security Centre alert, “Disruptive cyber activity highlights risk from internet-exposed systems and edge devices” - Published 27 Aug 2026; the NCSC says it has been engaging affected sectors directly ahead of publication

item.title: [High] A ransomware affiliate ran an AI coding agent inside victim networks — and the exposed server shows exactly how
item.category: Threat Intel — Ransomware tradecraft, AI-assisted intrusion
item.description: CloudSEK published analysis on 27 August of a misconfigured server belonging to a Russian-speaking Aurora ransomware affiliate, exposing tooling, command history, credential material and the operator’s Cursor chat transcripts. The campaign ran from April to July 2026 across nine countries; the operator reached domain-level or interactive access at 17 organisations, and four appeared on Aurora’s leak site. Manufacturing, food, agriculture and professional-services organisations were among those affected. The notable detail is not that AI was used but where: the transcripts show the assistant helping plan Active Directory escalation and intrusion steps, compressing the time between initial access and domain control. For a manufacturer the practical question is whether the identity used by IT administrators can reach the engineering workstations and the MES, because this operator’s route was domain privilege, not an ICS exploit. - CloudSEK research published 27 Aug 2026 — corroborated by GBHackers and Cybersecurity News - Research published 27 Aug 2026; the intrusion activity it documents ran April to July 2026

item.title: [Critical] Manufacturing took 747 of the 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in the second quarter
item.category: Threat intel — Manufacturing share of industrial ransomware
item.description: Dragos counted 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in Q2 2026, up around 12 percent on Q1, with manufacturing absorbing the clear majority. The analysis is blunt about mechanism: attackers did not need control-system access to stop production. Encrypting ERP, MES, quality systems, label printing, shipping and scheduling halts a line just as effectively as touching a PLC, and it is far easier. The Data I/O disclosure this month is the same story from the inside — production stopped as a containment decision on IT systems, not because a controller was manipulated. Manufacturers who scope OT security around the control network alone are defending the part attackers are not aiming at. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Dragos and Help Net Security - Report covers Q2 2026; published and reported 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, with critical manufacturing named
item.category: Threat intel — Joint federal advisory naming critical manufacturing
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-231A from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA describes actors using AI assistance to turn a well-documented open-source S7 library into custom tooling that queries internet-exposed Siemens S7 controllers in traffic resembling legitimate monitoring. Critical manufacturing is among the named sectors, and the agencies assess the activity as reconnaissance and pre-positioning rather than manipulation. The change worth internalising is not a new exploit. Writing a working S7 query used to require someone who knew the protocol; it no longer does, which enlarges the population capable of interrogating an exposed SIMATIC controller and makes obscurity a much weaker control than it was. - NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A — via CISA, BleepingComputer and Industrial Cyber - AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026; builds on AA26-097A from April 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
item.category: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings
item.description: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes paired red-team results from two critical-infrastructure organisations assessed with comparable tradecraft. One detected and responded; the other never noticed a domain compromise. The advisory is unusually direct that the difference was not product spend — both had capable tooling, but only one reviewed the output, correlated identity events and had practised the response. Manufacturers recognise the pattern because engineering workstations, MES servers and corporate laptops so often share one Active Directory, and because plant-floor systems are frequently excluded from whatever monitoring exists on the grounds that alerts would be noisy. - CISA advisory AA26-237A — corroborated by CyberScoop and The Hacker News - Published 25 Aug 2026; verified against the CISA advisory 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
item.category: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue
item.description: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch that included NetScaler. None is an ICS product, and after the Boston Scientific and Data I/O outages that is the pattern worth noticing: what stops manufacturing is usually the layer under it. CVE-2026-53362 is a Linux kernel flaw, and the MES server, historian, machine-vision appliance, protocol gateway and OT network sensor in most plants are Linux underneath, frequently as vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s timetable. CVE-2026-66384 is a path traversal in JFrog Artifactory — directly relevant in manufacturing, where Artifactory commonly stages firmware, container images and automation packages that end up on the plant floor. CVE-2023-49105 is an ownCloud authentication bypass patched since late 2023; exposed instances are usually unowned. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition, corroborated by Security Affairs and SecurityWeek - Added to KEV 27 Aug 2026; ownCloud flaw originally disclosed Nov 2023

item.title: [Critical] A seven-year-old SQL Server flaw is now confirmed exploited — and it is the database under your historian
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, historian and MES databases
item.description: CISA added six vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, and the one that matters most on the plant floor is CVE-2019-1068, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft SQL Server patched in July 2019 and only now confirmed as exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation runs code under the SQL Server Database Engine service account; where that account is over-privileged — which is common on systems installed by an integrator years ago — the attacker moves off the database and onto the Windows host. On a plant network this is the database under the historian, the MES, the batch or recipe store and the quality system — frequently an instance a machine builder or integrator installed as part of a line and left at the build it shipped with, sitting on the same flat network as the engineering workstations. No public write-up of the in-the-wild technique has appeared, so detection guidance is thin; the federal remediation deadline is 29 August. Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452 was added in the same batch. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 — corroborated by The Hacker News and Infosecurity Magazine - Added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; original Microsoft patch July 2019; federal remediation deadline 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from a patching recommendation to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, requiring no authentication, and reachable when the appliance runs as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre saw indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept appeared. In manufacturing, NetScaler routinely fronts the remote access used by engineers, third-shift support and the machine builders who dial in to diagnose equipment. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 and Citrix security bulletin — corroborated by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and watchTowr Labs analysis - Vendor patches released August 2026; exploitation indications from 17 Aug; added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Two unauthenticated flaws in Veeam ONE 13 — the monitoring layer that watches the backups you would restore from
item.category: Advisory — Backup and monitoring infrastructure, unauthenticated
item.description: Veeam disclosed vulnerabilities in Veeam ONE 13 in knowledge-base articles published on 25 August. CVE-2026-64633 is rated CVSS v4.0 10.0 and allows remote, unauthenticated code execution on the Veeam ONE agent host; CVE-2026-65641 is rated 9.3 and lets a remote unauthenticated attacker coerce SMB authentication out of the Veeam ONE service account, which is the first step in relaying that account somewhere more useful. Veeam ONE 13.x is affected and the 12.x line is not. In a plant Veeam ONE usually watches the backups of the MES, the historian and the engineering workstations that hold your PLC project files — the recovery capability that decides whether a ransomware event costs you a shift or a fortnight. There is no report of exploitation yet, but backup and monitoring servers are a standing target precisely because compromising them removes the recovery option before the ransomware runs. - Veeam knowledge-base articles KB4905 and KB4892 — corroborated by CyberScoop and Cybersecurity News - Vendor advisory published 25 Aug 2026; patched builds available the same day

item.title: [Critical] The Git server holding your PLC projects just went into KEV — Gitea is being exploited in the wild
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, engineering toolchain
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August after reports of active exploitation. Rated CVSS 9.8, it lets anyone with ordinary repository write access plant an executable Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Gitea 1.27.1 fixed it on 27 July; exploitation followed within a month. Self-hosted Gitea has become common in controls engineering because it is trivial to stand up inside a plant network for PLC projects, HMI screens, robot programs and configuration baselines. That convenience is the risk: a low-privilege contractor account converts into code execution on the machine holding the authoritative copy of your production logic. Federal remediation was due 28 August. - CISA KEV catalogue addition — corroborated by Help Net Security, SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Gitea 1.27.1 released 27 Jul 2026; advisory 28 Jul; added to KEV 25 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CVSS 10.0 on a Siemens edge gateway — unauthenticated code execution on a dual-homed device
item.category: Advisory — Maximum severity, Siemens edge gateway
item.description: Siemens’ August advisory set includes a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices, allowing a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute code with elevated privileges. Ten Siemens advisories arrived in the batch alongside Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact publications, and CISA published companion advisories the same week. The reason to prioritise this above other maximum-severity items is placement. Edge gateways are deployed specifically to move machine data from the line out to a historian, an analytics platform or an OEM cloud service, which makes them dual-homed by design and often the one device with a route in both directions. - Siemens ProductCERT August 2026 advisories and the CISA ICS advisory batch — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] No login required and no patch coming — the Ebyte gateway advisory is a replacement decision
item.category: Advisory — Serial-to-Ethernet gateway, no vendor patch
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-237-06 covers the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, whose web management interface does not consistently enforce authentication before granting administrative functionality. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read configuration, change settings, hijack sessions or disrupt device operation. CISA notes the vendor acknowledged the reports and said a patch was in development, then stopped responding, so no fix status exists. Cheap serial converters like this are endemic in manufacturing: they are what got a legacy press, oven, torque controller, scale or test rig onto the network, and they are almost never in a patch programme or an asset register. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-237-06, reported by researcher Jithin Nambiar — via CISA - Published 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026 — no vendor patch announced

item.title: [Info] From 11 September 2026 manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours
item.category: Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligation
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations begin on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability in their product, or a severe incident affecting its security, within 24 hours of becoming aware — with a fuller report following. The obligation lands on the manufacturer, so it applies to industrial firms that build machinery, instruments or connected equipment as well as to software vendors. The practical difficulty is rarely the report itself; it is that a 24-hour clock requires a detection and decision path that most engineering organisations have never had to build. - EU Regulation 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act) and European Commission implementation guidance - Regulation entered into force 10 Dec 2024; reporting obligations apply from 11 Sep 2026; full application 11 Dec 2027; status verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] The NSA is putting an ISA/IEC 62443 certificate in front of the controllers it buys
item.description: ISASecure announced a partnership with the National Security Agency to develop a High Criticality Component Security Assurance certification scheme, derived from its Component Security Assurance programme and grounded in ISA/IEC 62443-4-2. Once accepted, the NSA intends to use it when adding OT components to the National Security Systems product compliant list. For manufacturers this cuts both ways, which is what makes it worth watching. As a buyer, it gives you a citable standard for the next machine or controller specification. As a builder of connected equipment, it is an early signal of what large customers will start demanding in their own tenders. - ISA / ISASecure press release — corroborated by Automation World and ISSSource - Announced 20 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026
